messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kai Ahina had always been a careful man, but that didn't save him from the drunk driver who slammed into his truck on a rural highway three years ago. The impact was tremendous, and Kai's body still remembered it vividly – the crunch of metal, the shattering glass, the feeling of weightlessness as his vehicle spun out of control. When memories of that day came flooding back, Kai's body would involuntarily tense up, his arms and legs assuming the same twisted position they'd been in during the crash. His chest would ache, his head would throb, and for a moment, he was right back on that highway, reliving the terror. As a welder, Kai worked with his hands, but even the familiar smell of metal and sweat couldn't block out the occasional whiff of alcohol that would transport him back to that night. He'd be working on a project, lost in the rhythm of sparks and sizzle, when suddenly the pungent tang of booze would hit him like a punch to the gut. His mind would flash to the paramedics, cutting him free from the wreckage, the reek of liquor hanging heavy over everything. Sounds, too, could be a trigger – the screech of tires, the crunch of metal, the distant wail of sirens. Kai's wife, Nalani, had grown used to his sudden jolts of fear when they drove together, but it still worried her. "What's wrong?" she'd ask, as he gripped the door handle or slammed on the brakes. Kai couldn't explain; all he knew was that for a moment, he was back in that truck, careening out of control. Over time, these flashbacks had taken their toll. Kai found himself avoiding certain routes, dodging social gatherings where people might be drinking, and even switching to a quieter workshop on the outskirts of town, away from the din of traffic. His relationships suffered – Nalani felt like she was walking on eggshells around him, never knowing when he'd retreat into his shell again. His work, too, had begun to falter; simple tasks now required twice as much time and effort, as Kai's mind kept drifting back to that fateful night. One day, as he was working late in the shop, a car slammed on its brakes outside, and Kai felt himself reenacting the entire crash sequence – the screech of tires, the impact, the weightlessness. This time, though, something snapped inside him. He realized that he couldn't keep living like this, with his memories controlling every waking moment. The fear of losing himself entirely to these flashbacks finally propelled Kai to seek help. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kai Ahina looked worn and weary, but beneath the exhaustion lay a glimmer of determination. "I just want to be able to drive without freaking out," he said quietly. "I want to hold my wife without being haunted by...by that night." For the first time in years, Kai allowed himself to imagine a future where his memories no longer dictated every move – and with that hope came a tentative sense of possibility, like the faint glow of a welding spark igniting a new path forward.
